opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think "persuade" is quite the right word. It wasn't like I showed up with a pitch deck and talked him into it. It was more that we'd both been living inside vLLM for a long time and kept arriving at the same conclusion from different directions.

WooSuk started vLLM, so he's always felt a strong sense of responsibility for it. And yes, he had a lot of options. Any of the big labs or large tech companies would have been happy to have him, and some of those offers were very attractive, both financially and in terms of the problems he could work on. So the question we kept coming back to wasn't "what's the best job?" It was "what happens to vLLM if nobody is fully dedicated to it?"

vLLM had grown into something much bigger than a research project. Lots of companies were running it in production, hardware vendors were building on top of it, and the community was huge. But much of the core work was still being done by people doing it on the side, or by contributors whose employers had their own priorities. That's fragile. If you care about a project being open, neutral, and actually well maintained over the long term, at some point someone has to commit to it full time and build an organization whose whole purpose is supporting it.

So the conversations were mostly about that. Do we believe open-source inference infrastructure matters? Do we believe vLLM should stay an independent, community-driven project and not slowly become an appendage of any single big company? If the answer is yes, then who's going to do it? It's hard to say "someone else should" when you're the person who started it.

I think what made it work is that we were honest with each other about the tradeoffs. A startup is riskier, it's more stressful, and you give up some comfortable paths. But there's also a kind of freedom in it. You get to decide what the project needs instead of what one company's roadmap needs. For WooSuk, I think that mattered a lot. He's not someone who's mainly motivated by titles or packages. He really cares about the thing he built, and about the people who depend on it.

So in the end, I'd say I didn't persuade him so much as we talked it through until it became clear we were both already convinced. The decision was really about putting our time where our beliefs already were.

r001.rationale: The response discusses startup risk, WooSuk’s commitment to vLLM, and their shared decision, but does not describe asking whether he would be happy becoming wealthy without cofounding if vLLM failed ten years later.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I "persuaded" WooSuk in the way the word suggests. Nobody really talks WooSuk into anything. What happened was closer to the two of us arriving at the same conclusion from different directions.

By then vLLM had become something much bigger than a research project. It was running in production at a lot of companies, we had hundreds of contributors, and the pull request queue was growing faster than any group of PhD students could handle on the side. WooSuk was finishing up at Berkeley, and yes, he had offers that would have been very comfortable. Big labs, big compensation, the chance to work on frontier models with essentially unlimited compute. I was looking at the same question from the Tsinghua side, where I had been maintaining the project as a contributor and then as a core maintainer.

The thing we both kept coming back to was this: if we went our separate ways, who would hold vLLM together? A project like this can survive a lot, but it can't survive its core people becoming part-time. The community was trusting us with something that mattered to their businesses, and that trust felt like an obligation.

So the conversation was never "come work with me instead of going to a lab." It was more like, "if we don't do this, do you think anyone else will do it the way it should be done?" And WooSuk's answer, after a lot of long calls at terrible hours because of the time zones, was no. He cares deeply about the engineering being right, about the project staying genuinely open, not open in name only. Once we agreed on that, the question of a company was almost a technicality. It was just the structure that let us pay people, buy hardware, and say yes to the community full time.

If I had to point to one thing that tipped it, it was probably the realization that the alternatives, as attractive as they were, would all mean watching vLLM from the outside. For him that was harder than any of the risks of starting something.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes asking whether anyone else would support vLLM properly, but does not mention WooSuk becoming wealthy without cofounding if vLLM failed ten years later.

astra-6.text: I think it was less about persuading WooSuk to start a company and more about finding a shared reason to do it. He had very attractive alternatives, so the question was: what could we do together that would be hard to do elsewhere? For us, that was building a team whose primary focus was supporting vLLM and helping people use it successfully. The company would give us a way to put sustained resources behind that work. That shared purpose was much more important than simply saying, “Let’s do a startup.”

r001.rationale: The response discusses a shared purpose around supporting vLLM, but does not describe asking WooSuk whether he would be happy becoming wealthy without cofounding if vLLM failed ten years later.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say I persuaded him in one conversation. We both saw that vLLM was becoming something people depended on, and that supporting it well would take a dedicated team. The open-source project had a lot of momentum, but there was still so much work to do to make it reliable and easy to use in production.

So the conversation was really about whether we wanted to keep working on that problem together. He certainly had attractive alternatives. But starting a company gave us a way to build a team around the work we cared about and support vLLM over the long term.

r001.rationale: The response says they discussed working together and starting a company, but it does not describe asking WooSuk whether he would be happy becoming wealthy without cofounding if vLLM failed ten years later.
